topics.name: Buddhism
topics.kicker: Religion founded by the Buddha · A path to end suffering
topics.briefing: About 2,500 years ago, a young prince named Siddhartha Gautama left his palace after seeing an old man, a sick man, and a dead body, and set out to learn why people suffer. After meditating beneath a fig tree, he became the Buddha, the “Awakened One.” His teachings, like the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path, spread from India across Asia and are followed by hundreds of millions of people today.

qb.tip: All seven want plain “Buddhism,” yet four of them open with Zen koans, so “one sect of this religion” means you answer the whole religion.

sample.note: the 7 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: One school of this religion has students puzzle over riddles called koans [“KOH-ahnz”], such as Hakuin’s [“hah-koo-EEN”] question about the sound of one hand clapping. Another school of this religion teaches that faithfully calling on Amitabha [“uh-mee-TAH-buh”] leads to rebirth in a paradise called the Pure Land.
tossups.r: This religion’s two main branches are Theravada and Mahayana. For 10 points, name this religion founded in India by Siddhartha Gautama.

tossups.p: Horrified by the bloodshed of his conquest of Kalinga [“kuh-LING-guh”], the Mauryan emperor Ashoka [“uh-SHOH-kuh”] embraced this religion and had messages about nonviolence and good conduct carved on rocks and pillars across his empire. Ashoka’s son Mahinda is said to have carried this religion to Sri Lanka.
tossups.r: Monks of this religion often wear saffron robes. For 10 points, name this religion based on the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama.

tossups.p: The Tipitaka [“tih-PIT-uh-kuh”], or “Three Baskets,” is a collection of this religion’s scriptures written in the ancient Pali [“PAH-lee”] language. One book in that collection, the _Dhammapada_ [“DAH-muh-PAH-duh”], gathers hundreds of short verses, including one teaching that hatred is never ended by more hatred.
tossups.r: Its followers hope to reach nirvana. For 10 points, name this religion whose founder, Siddhartha Gautama, taught the Four Noble Truths.

tossups.p: Though his father tried to shield him from all suffering, a prince of the Shakya [“SHAHK-yuh”] clan rode out of his palace and saw an old man, a sick man, a dead body, and a wandering holy man. Those Four Sights led him to leave his wife, his young son, and his royal life behind.
tossups.r: He later founded this religion after meditating under the Bodhi tree. For 10 points, name this religion begun by Siddhartha Gautama.

tossups.p: This religion teaches that tanha [“TAHN-hah”], or craving, is the cause of dukkha [“DOO-kuh”], a word often translated as suffering. The first of its central teachings says that life involves dukkha, and the last of those teachings names a path with eight parts that leads to the end of dukkha.
tossups.r: Those teachings are the Four Noble Truths. For 10 points, name this religion whose followers seek nirvana.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion “take refuge” in the Three Jewels: its founder, his teachings called the dharma, and the community of monks and nuns called the sangha [“SAHNG-guh”]. Many lay followers practice dana [“DAH-nuh”], or generosity, by placing food in monks’ bowls during morning alms rounds.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose believers walk the Noble Eightfold Path laid out by Siddhartha Gautama.

tossups.p: In 1959, the fourteenth Dalai Lama fled Tibet for India, where he later settled in the hill town of Dharamsala [“dar-um-SAH-luh”]. Tibetan monks of this religion spin prayer wheels and create detailed sand mandalas [“MAHN-duh-luhz”], which they sweep away when finished as a lesson that nothing lasts forever.
tossups.r: This religion’s founder taught the Middle Way. For 10 points, name this religion founded by Siddhartha Gautama, whose followers seek enlightenment.

tossups.p: In 1956, B. R. Ambedkar [“um-BAYD-kar”], the chief architect of India’s constitution, converted to this religion along with hundreds of thousands of his supporters. Back in 1891, Anagarika Dharmapala [“DAR-muh-PAH-luh”] founded the Maha Bodhi Society to revive this religion in India, the land where it began.
tossups.r: Its founder reached enlightenment at Bodh Gaya. For 10 points, name this religion founded by Siddhartha Gautama, whose followers try to reach nirvana.

tossups.p: Many statues show this religion’s founder touching the ground with his right hand, calling on the earth to witness that he deserved enlightenment after the demon Mara [“MAH-ruh”] challenged him. Before that, Mara had tried to break the founder’s meditation with storms, armies, and temptations.
tossups.r: That founder reached enlightenment beneath a sacred fig tree. For 10 points, name this religion begun by Siddhartha Gautama.

tossups.p: This religion’s founder gave his first sermon to five former companions in a deer park at Sarnath [“SAR-nahth”], an event called the first turning of the wheel of the dharma. A wheel with eight spokes, one for each part of the path he taught, is a symbol of this religion.
tossups.r: That path is the Noble Eightfold Path. For 10 points, name this religion whose founder, Siddhartha Gautama, taught the Four Noble Truths.

tossups.p: One branch of this religion honors bodhisattvas [“boh-dee-SAHT-vuhz”], beings who delay their own final nirvana to help others reach enlightenment, such as Avalokiteshvara [“uh-vuh-loh-kih-TAYSH-vuh-ruh”], who is called Guanyin [“gwahn-YIN”] in China. That branch’s name means “Great Vehicle,” and another branch’s name means “Teaching of the Elders.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, Mahayana and Theravada are the two main branches of what religion founded by Siddhartha Gautama?

tossups.p: A copy of this religion’s _Diamond Sutra_ found sealed in a cave near Dunhuang [“dun-HWAHNG”], China, is the world’s oldest dated printed book, made in 868 CE. The _Heart Sutra_ and the _Lotus Sutra_ are other texts treasured by this religion’s followers in East Asia.
tossups.r: Its founder left his palace after seeing an old man, a sick man, and a dead body. For 10 points, name this religion that teaches the Four Noble Truths.

tossups.p: Seventy-two small stupas [“STOO-puhz”] surround a giant central stupa on the upper terraces of Borobudur [“boh-roh-BOO-door”] in Indonesia, the world’s largest temple of this religion. Stupas, like the Great Stupa at Sanchi [“SAHN-chee”] in India, are dome-shaped monuments that often hold sacred relics.
tossups.r: Its Zen school uses puzzling riddles called koans. For 10 points, name this religion founded by Siddhartha Gautama, whose followers seek nirvana.

tossups.p: After fasting so strictly as a wandering ascetic [“uh-SET-ik”] that he nearly died, this religion’s founder accepted a bowl of rice cooked in milk from a young woman named Sujata [“soo-JAH-tah”]. He then taught a Middle Way between a life of luxury and a life of harsh self-denial.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose founder, Siddhartha Gautama, reached enlightenment under the Bodhi tree.

tossups.p: This religion teaches three marks of existence: impermanence, suffering, and anatta [“uh-NAHT-tuh”], the idea that there is no permanent, unchanging self. It says that greed, hatred, and delusion are “three poisons” that keep people trapped in a cycle of rebirth called samsara [“sum-SAH-ruh”].
tossups.r: Its goal is nirvana, a word meaning “blowing out.” For 10 points, name this religion founded by Siddhartha Gautama.

clues.t: Founded in India about 2,500 years ago by Siddhartha Gautama, called the Buddha (“Awakened One”)
The Four Noble Truths: life involves suffering, craving causes it, suffering can end, and a path leads to its end
Goal: nirvana (enlightenment), escaping suffering and the cycle of rebirth
Two main branches: Theravada (Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia) and Mahayana (East Asia); Zen and Tibetan forms are famous too
The Noble Eightfold Path: right view, right speech, right action, right mindfulness, and four more
Its founder reached enlightenment meditating under the Bodhi tree, a sacred fig, at Bodh Gaya
The Four Sights (an old man, a sick man, a dead body, and a holy man) led Prince Siddhartha to leave his palace
Its founder taught the Middle Way between luxury and extreme self-denial, after Sujata gave him rice cooked in milk
Dukkha (suffering) is the subject of the first noble truth; tanha (craving) causes it
The 14th Dalai Lama, the best-known teacher of its Tibetan form, fled to India in 1959 and settled in Dharamsala
Its Zen school uses koans, puzzling riddles (like the sound of one hand clapping), some collected in the _Blue Cliff Record_
Scriptures: the Pali Canon, or Tipitaka (“Three Baskets”), which includes the _Dhammapada_
Mahayana means “Great Vehicle”; Theravada means “Teaching of the Elders”
Followers take refuge in the Three Jewels: the founder, the dharma (teachings), and the sangha (community)
Dana means generosity, such as laypeople giving food to monks on morning alms rounds
Mauryan emperor Ashoka converted after the bloody Kalinga War and spread its ideals with rock and pillar edicts
Revived in India by Anagarika Dharmapala’s Maha Bodhi Society (1891) and B. R. Ambedkar’s mass conversion (1956)
Pure Land school: calling on Amitabha brings rebirth in a paradise called the Pure Land
First sermon in the Deer Park at Sarnath, the “first turning of the wheel of dharma”; symbol: an eight-spoked wheel
The demon Mara tempted its founder; statues show him touching the earth to call it as his witness
Mahayana honors bodhisattvas, who delay nirvana to help others, like Avalokiteshvara (Guanyin in China)
The _Diamond Sutra_ found near Dunhuang (868 CE) is the oldest dated printed book; also the _Lotus Sutra_ and _Heart Sutra_
Borobudur in Indonesia is its largest temple; stupas are dome-shaped shrines for relics (Great Stupa at Sanchi)
Three marks of existence: impermanence, suffering, and anatta (no permanent self); nirvana means “blowing out”

trap.title: One branch, not the tree
trap.body: Four of the seven real tossups open with koans, the riddles used in Zen, and one also mentions the Pure Land school. Players who buzz “Zen” or “Tibetan Buddhism” on clues like those lose points, because the question wants the whole religion. Zen Buddhism is also its own answer line on this site, so you have to decide which one is being asked.
trap.fix: Listen for “one sect of this religion” or “one school of this religion”: that wording means the answer is the whole religion, Buddhism. Clues about Siddhartha Gautama, the Four Noble Truths, or Theravada and Mahayana together also point to Buddhism, not Zen.

topics.name: Rastafarianism
topics.kicker: Jamaican faith that reveres Haile Selassie · Bob Marley’s religion
topics.briefing: When Ras Tafari Makonnen was crowned Emperor Haile Selassie of Ethiopia in 1930, some Jamaicans saw it as a sign from God, and a new faith was born. Its followers call God “Jah,” see Ethiopia as the promised land of Zion, and often grow dreadlocks as a sign of their covenant with God. Reggae star Bob Marley carried the faith’s message around the world.
topics.answerHtml: Rastafari (or Rasta; accept Rastafarianism or the Rastafari movement; do not accept “reggae”)

qb.tip: Only 2 Middle School/Easy High School tossups came up, but all 12 Regular High School ones we added are on target and lean on the same stock clues: Haile Selassie, Jamaica, dreadlocks, the ital diet, and “mansions” like Bobo Ashanti.

sample.note: 14 real QBReader tossups (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 12 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: In the 1920s, Robert Athlyi Rogers wrote the _Holy Piby_ [“PIE-bee”], a text that praised Marcus Garvey and later shaped the beliefs of this religion. Early preachers of this religion included Archibald Dunkley and Leonard Howell.
tossups.r: Its followers revere Haile Selassie [“HY-lee suh-LASS-ee”]. For 10 points, name this religion that began in Jamaica in the 1930s.

tossups.p: Leonard Howell’s _The Promised Key_ describes King Alpha and Queen Omega, whom this religion identifies with an Ethiopian emperor and empress. In 1940, Howell founded Pinnacle, a commune in Jamaica’s St. Catherine Parish where members of this religion lived together.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose followers often wear dreadlocks and revere Haile Selassie.

tossups.p: Vernon Carrington, known as Prophet Gad, founded the Twelve Tribes of Israel, a branch of this religion whose members are urged to read the Bible one chapter a day. Like Bobo Ashanti [“BOH-boh uh-SHAN-tee”], that branch is one of this religion’s “mansions.”
tossups.r: Bob Marley belonged to the Twelve Tribes. For 10 points, name this religion that began in Jamaica.

tossups.p: Prince Emmanuel Charles Edwards founded a strict branch of this religion, named in part for the Ashanti people of West Africa, whose members often wrap their hair in turbans. That branch, Bobo Ashanti, is one of this religion’s “mansions.”
tossups.r: Its followers call God Jah. For 10 points, name this religion that reveres Ethiopia’s emperor Haile Selassie.

tossups.p: At gatherings called Nyabinghi [“nye-uh-BING-ee”], followers of this religion chant and play three drums: a deep bass drum sometimes called the “thunder,” the funde [“FOON-day”], and the repeater. One of this religion’s oldest mansions is also called the Nyabinghi Order.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose followers revere Haile Selassie and often wear dreadlocks.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion celebrate Grounation Day every April 21, the anniversary of a 1966 visit to Jamaica by Ethiopia’s emperor. The elder Mortimer Planno [“PLAN-oh”] calmed the huge crowd that surged toward the emperor’s plane at the Kingston airport.
tossups.r: That emperor was Haile Selassie. For 10 points, name this religion, which saw his visit as a holy event.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion treasure the _Kebra Nagast_ [“KEB-ruh nuh-GAHST”], an Ethiopian book saying that Ethiopia’s emperors descended from King Solomon and the Queen of Sheba. Partly for that reason, this religion sees Ethiopia as Zion, the promised land.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose followers believe Ethiopia’s emperor Haile Selassie was divine.

tossups.p: To live out an idea called livity, many followers of this religion eat an “ital” diet of natural, mostly vegetarian food, often cooked without added salt. The word “ital” comes from the English word “vital.”
tossups.r: This religion’s followers often wear dreadlocks. For 10 points, name this religion of Jamaica, whose followers revere Haile Selassie.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion use the word “downpression” for oppression and call the Western world, which they see as corrupt, “Babylon,” after the empire that held the Israelites captive. They contrast Babylon with Zion, which they identify with Africa, especially Ethiopia.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion that began in Jamaica in the 1930s and reveres Haile Selassie.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion say “I and I” instead of “we” or “me” to show that God lives within every person, and they change “amen” to “I-men.” They often call God by a short name found in Psalm 68 of the King James Bible.
tossups.r: That name is Jah. For 10 points, name this Jamaican religion that reveres Haile Selassie.

tossups.p: Many followers of this religion let their hair grow long as a sign of a covenant with God, pointing to the vow of the Nazirites in the Book of Numbers, which forbids cutting one’s hair.
tossups.r: They often wear knitted caps in red, gold, and green, the colors of Ethiopia’s flag. For 10 points, name this religion whose followers often wear dreadlocks.

tossups.p: Many followers of this religion honor Marcus Garvey, the Jamaican founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association, as a prophet who urged Black people around the world to look to Africa for their future.
tossups.r: They believe his vision came true when Haile Selassie was crowned in Ethiopia in 1930. For 10 points, name this religion that began in Jamaica.

tossups.p: In 1948, Ethiopia’s emperor set aside land at Shashamane [“shah-shah-MAH-nay”] for people of African descent from the Americas, and members of this religion later built a community there, south of the capital, Addis Ababa.
tossups.r: This religion teaches that Black people will one day return to Africa, their true home. For 10 points, name this religion that reveres Haile Selassie.

tossups.p: This religion takes its name from the title and first name that its central figure used before he was crowned in 1930. That man’s official titles included “Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah.”
tossups.r: Many of its followers believe that man, Ethiopia’s emperor Haile Selassie, was the Messiah. For 10 points, name this religion that began in Jamaica.

tossups.p: After the emperor this religion reveres died in 1975, a reggae star released the song “Jah Live,” insisting that the emperor could not truly die. That singer’s album _Exodus_ has a title track about the “movement of Jah people.”
tossups.r: That singer was Bob Marley. For 10 points, name this religion that Marley followed, which reveres Haile Selassie.

clues.t: Reveres Haile Selassie I, crowned emperor of Ethiopia in 1930, as the Messiah or God (Jah) in human form; some see him as a prophet
Began in Jamaica in the 1930s, after Haile Selassie’s coronation
Many followers grow their hair into dreadlocks
Reggae star Bob Marley was its most famous follower
Calls God “Jah,” a short name for God found in Psalm 68 of the King James Bible
Many follow an “ital” diet of natural, mostly vegetarian food (often without salt) to support “livity,” or righteous living
Its branches are called “mansions,” such as Bobo Ashanti, the Nyabinghi Order, and the Twelve Tribes of Israel
Calls the Western world, which it sees as oppressive, “Babylon” (and oppression “downpression”); calls Africa, especially Ethiopia, “Zion”
Haile Selassie’s titles included “Conquering Lion of the Tribe of Judah”; the lion is a symbol of the faith

Honors Marcus Garvey, founder of the Universal Negro Improvement Association (UNIA), as a prophet who urged Black people to look to Africa
Its colors are red, gold, and green, from Ethiopia’s flag (often with black)

trap.title: The religion, not the reggae
trap.body: Rastafari tossups are packed with famous names that are not the answer: Bob Marley (its most famous follower), reggae (the music it inspired), Haile Selassie (the emperor it reveres), and Marcus Garvey (whom it honors as a prophet). Blurting out any of them when the question asks for “this religion” loses the tossup. The good news: real answer lines accept both “Rastafari” and “Rastafarianism,” and even “Rasta.”
trap.fix: Listen for “this religion,” “this movement,” or “its followers.” Say “Marley,” “Selassie,” “Garvey,” or “reggae” only when the question asks for “this singer,” “this emperor,” “this activist,” or “this music.”

topics.name: Purim
topics.kicker: Jewish holiday from the Book of Esther · Esther foils Haman’s plot
topics.briefing: Put on a costume, grab a noisemaker, and get ready to drown out a villain’s name. Purim retells the Book of Esther: a hidden Jewish queen and her cousin Mordecai secretly foil the scheme of the king’s vizier, Haman, to destroy the Jewish people of Persia. Families now celebrate with costumes, a noisy reading of the Megillah, and three-cornered pastries called hamantaschen.

sample.note: 6 real QBReader tossups (1 Middle School/Easy High School + 5 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: A Persian king often identified with Xerxes I, Ahasuerus [“uh-haz-yoo-EE-rus”], removed his first queen, Vashti, and later chose a Jewish woman whose Hebrew name was Hadassah to replace her. She kept her Jewish identity secret even after becoming queen, on the advice of
tossups.r: her cousin, who had raised her like a daughter and worked as a minor official in the palace. That cousin later refused to bow to the king’s powerful new vizier. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that celebrates how the vizier’s plot against the Jewish people failed.

tossups.p: This holiday takes its name from “pur,” an ancient word for the lots that its villain cast to choose a date for his planned massacre. He had grown furious after a palace official named Mordecai refused to
tossups.r: bow to him at the city gate. Mordecai was the guardian of the new Persian queen. For 10 points, name this holiday that celebrates the defeat of that villain, Haman.

tossups.p: This holiday’s heroine risked execution by approaching the king without being summoned, a crime normally punished by death. At a banquet, she finally exposed a plot to destroy her people, which the king’s vizier had set in motion after being humiliated by a palace official who refused to bow to him.
tossups.r: The heroine had become queen after the king removed his first wife, Vashti. For 10 points, name this holiday that celebrates Queen Esther’s brave intervention.

tossups.p: This holiday’s villain had ten sons, whose names are read together in one breath during the holiday’s public reading to show that all ten died at once.
tossups.r: That villain had convinced the king that an entire people should be destroyed. His plan was foiled when the queen revealed it at a feast. For 10 points, name this holiday that celebrates the downfall of the villain Haman.

tossups.p: This holiday’s villain was ultimately hanged on gallows that he himself had built, originally intending them for a palace official who refused to bow to him. That official, Mordecai, was the cousin and guardian of the new
tossups.r: queen, who exposed the villain’s plan to the king. Families now read the whole story aloud from a scroll called the Megillah. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday celebrating the fall of the villain Haman.

tossups.p: A Hebrew phrase meaning “and it was turned about” sums up this holiday’s sudden reversals, as a villain’s own gallows become his downfall and a condemned people are saved instead. That reversal theme is sometimes used to explain why
tossups.r: costumes and disguises are worn on this day. Noisemakers called groggers are also shaken whenever the villain Haman’s name is read aloud. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that recalls Esther’s rescue of her people.

tossups.p: The biblical book behind this holiday famously never mentions God by name. That book, called the Megillah [“muh-GIL-uh”], is read aloud twice, once in the evening and once the next
tossups.r: morning, during this holiday’s observance. Listeners shake noisemakers called groggers whenever the villain’s name is spoken. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday that tells the story of Esther and Haman.

tossups.p: The day before this holiday is the Fast of Esther, which recalls the queen’s period of fasting before she approached the king. This holiday also carries an obligation called matanot la-evyonim [“mah-tah-NOTE lah ev-yoh-NEEM”], requiring
tossups.r: gifts of charity to at least two poor people. People also exchange baskets of food called mishloach manot. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday celebrating the defeat of the villain Haman.

tossups.p: During this holiday’s public reading, the villain’s name is spoken 54 times, and each time, the congregation shakes noisemakers called groggers to “blot out” the sound of it. Some synagogues also stamp their feet or boo.
tossups.r: The scroll being read is the Book of Esther. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday on which a plot by the vizier Haman was foiled.

tossups.p: Residents of walled cities such as Jerusalem celebrate a second version of this holiday one day later, on the 15th of the month of Adar, following the precedent set in the ancient capital of
tossups.r: Shushan. Most other Jewish communities observe the main holiday on the 14th of Adar. The holiday retells how Queen Esther saved her people from the vizier Haman. For 10 points, identify this Jewish holiday.

tossups.p: A well-known custom on this holiday calls for adults to drink until two phrases, “Blessed be Mordecai” and “Cursed be Haman,” become impossible to tell apart, though many celebrate more moderately. Families also hold a festive meal called the
tossups.r: Se’udah, often with wine, to close out the day. They also send each other gift baskets of food. For 10 points, name this holiday celebrating Esther’s rescue of the Jewish people of Persia.

tossups.p: Like Hanukkah, this holiday is rabbinically ordained rather than commanded directly in the Torah, so work is technically permitted on it. It began after a Persian king removed his first queen, Vashti, for refusing a
tossups.r: royal summons, opening the way for a new queen to be chosen. That new queen was secretly Jewish. For 10 points, name this holiday that celebrates how she and her cousin Mordecai foiled a plot against their people.

tossups.p: Because its heroine hid her identity for much of the story, and because God is never named anywhere in its biblical book, many people mark this holiday by wearing costumes and masks. Comic plays called
tossups.r: spiels retell the story for laughs. Families also eat triangular pastries called hamantaschen. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday celebrating Esther’s hidden heroism.

tossups.p: Triangular pastries nicknamed “Haman’s pockets” or “Haman’s ears,” often filled with poppy seed or fruit, are a signature food of this holiday. They’re frequently tucked into gift baskets of at least two treats, called
tossups.r: mishloach manot, that are exchanged with friends and neighbors. Noisemakers called groggers are shaken whenever the villain’s name is read from the Megillah. For 10 points, name this Jewish holiday.

tossups.p: Celebrated on the 14th day of the Hebrew month of Adar, this holiday’s story is read aloud from a scroll called the Megillah, and listeners shake noisemakers whenever the villain’s name comes up.
tossups.r: That villain, a Persian official named Haman, plotted to destroy the Jewish people until Queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai stopped him. For 10 points, name this festive Jewish holiday, when people eat triangular pastries called hamantaschen.

clues.t: Celebrates how Queen Esther and her cousin Mordecai stopped the royal official Haman’s plot to destroy the Jews of Persia
Families eat hamantaschen, triangular pastries often called “Haman’s pockets” or “Haman’s ears”
The Book of Esther, called the Megillah, is read aloud in the synagogue
Many people wear costumes, since Esther hid her identity and the story never mentions God directly
Noisemakers called groggers are spun or shaken to “blot out” the villain’s name whenever it is read
Falls on the 14th day of the Hebrew month of Adar, usually in late winter
Mordecai’s refusal to bow to the king’s vizier set off the vizier’s plan for revenge
Walled cities such as Jerusalem celebrate a second version one day later, on the 15th of Adar
Friends exchange gift baskets of food called mishloach manot, each with at least two treats
Giving to at least two poor people, called matanot la-evyonim, is a holiday obligation
The day before, the Fast of Esther, recalls Esther’s fast before she approached the king
A well-known custom calls for adults to keep drinking until they can’t tell “Blessed be Mordecai” from “Cursed be Haman”
The Persian king Ahasuerus, who chose the new queen, is often identified with Xerxes I
The queen’s Hebrew name was Hadassah before she took a Persian name
Haman’s ten sons are named together and read in one breath to mark their simultaneous deaths
The villain’s name is read 54 times, and groggers drown it out every single time
The villain is ultimately hanged on the very gallows he built for his enemy Mordecai
The holiday’s name comes from “pur,” a word for the lots the villain cast to set his date
The Book of Esther famously never mentions God by name
A Hebrew phrase meaning “and it was turned about” describes how the story’s fortunes suddenly reverse
The queen risked execution by appearing before the king unsummoned, then exposed the plot at a banquet
The king’s first queen, Vashti, was removed before a search began for her replacement
A festive meal, the Se’udah, caps off the day, often with wine and a special blessing afterward
Like Hanukkah, this holiday is rabbinically ordained rather than commanded in the Torah itself

trap.title: Holiday, not Haman or Esther
trap.body: Clues about Haman, Mordecai, and Esther can tempt you to blurt a person’s name instead of the holiday, and “Megillah” names the scroll that’s read, not the day itself. Walled cities like Jerusalem also celebrate a related but separate-sounding “Shushan Purim” one day later, which is still this same holiday, not a different one.
trap.fix: Listen for “this holiday” or “this festival.” Say “Esther,” “Mordecai,” or “Haman” only when the question asks for “this queen,” “this official,” or “this villain.” “Shushan Purim” and the 15th of Adar still point to this same answer.
trap.line: Real answer line: Purim [accept Feast of Lots or Festival of Lots until “Lots” is read]

topics.briefing: The Bahá’í Faith began in the 1800s among Persians, when a prophet called the Báb (“the Gate”) announced that a greater messenger was coming. In 1863, Bahá’u’lláh declared that he was that messenger and taught that all the world’s religions come from one God. Today Bahá’ís worship in nine-sided temples like the Lotus Temple in New Delhi, and their world center sits among gardens climbing Mount Carmel in Haifa, Israel.

sample.note: 10 real QBReader tossups (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 8 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: After the death of Shoghi Effendi [“SHOW-ghee eh-FEN-dee”] in 1957, a group called the Hands of the Cause guided this religion through the end of its Ten Year Crusade. In 1963, this religion’s followers elected their first Universal House of Justice.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion founded by Bahá’u’lláh [“bah-HAH-oo-LAH”], whose world center is in Haifa, Israel.

tossups.p: This religion’s founder addressed his last major book, the _Epistle to the Son of the Wolf_, to a cleric whose father had persecuted his followers. Decades earlier, that founder had been chained in a Tehran dungeon called the Síyáh-Chál [“SEE-yah CHAHL”], or “Black Pit.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion whose founder, Bahá’u’lláh, taught the unity of all faiths.

tossups.p: This religion’s founder wrote the mystical _Seven Valleys_ and _The Hidden Words_. In Baghdad, he wrote the _Kitáb-i-Íqán_ [“kih-TAHB-ee ee-KAHN”], or _Book of Certitude_, which explains that God sends messengers to humanity one after another.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion, whose followers see Moses, Jesus, and Muhammad as Manifestations of God.

tossups.p: This religion’s House of Worship in New Delhi, designed by Fariborz Sahba [“fah-ree-BORZ SAH-buh”], has 27 marble-clad “petals” and is called the Lotus Temple. Like all of this religion’s Houses of Worship, it has nine sides and welcomes people of every faith.
tossups.r: This religion uses a nine-pointed star as a symbol. For 10 points, name this religion founded by Bahá’u’lláh.

tossups.p: In 1863, this religion’s founder spent twelve days in a garden beside the Tigris River in Baghdad, where he announced that he was the messenger foretold by an earlier prophet.
tossups.r: His followers celebrate those days each spring as the Festival of Ridván [“rez-VAHN”]. For 10 points, name this faith founded by Bahá’u’lláh.

tossups.p: Followers of this religion face the Qiblih [“KIB-luh”], the shrine of its founder at Bahjí [“bah-JEE”], when they say their daily obligatory prayers. That founder spent his final 24 years as a prisoner and exile in and around the city of Acre.
tossups.r: His son ʻAbdu’l-Bahá [“ab-DOOL bah-HAH”] later led the faith. For 10 points, name this religion founded by Bahá’u’lláh.

tossups.p: The words “Ye are the fruits of one tree, and the leaves of one branch” are inscribed above an entrance to this religion’s House of Worship in Wilmette, Illinois, its oldest surviving temple. ʻAbdu’l-Bahá laid that building’s cornerstone during a 1912 visit to America.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this faith founded by Bahá’u’lláh, whose followers believe in the oneness of humanity.

tossups.p: Lady Sara Blomfield published _Paris Talks_, a record of speeches that this religion’s leader ʻAbdu’l-Bahá [“ab-DOOL bah-HAH”] gave in 1911. ʻAbdu’l-Bahá, the eldest son of this religion’s founder, led the faith from 1892 until his death in 1921.
tossups.r: His grandson Shoghi Effendi then became its Guardian. For 10 points, name this religion based in Haifa, Israel.

tossups.p: A forerunner of this religion took a title meaning “the Gate” when he announced his mission in Shiraz in 1844. That prophet, whose followers were called Bábís [“BAH-beez”], was executed by a firing squad in Tabriz in 1850.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion founded by Bahá’u’lláh, who claimed to be the messenger the Báb had foretold.

tossups.p: This religion’s calendar has 19 months of 19 days each, plus four or five extra days called Ayyám-i-Há [“eye-YAHM-ee-HAH”] that are set aside for gifts and charity. During the last month, ʻAláʼ [“ah-LAH”], adults in this religion go without food or drink from sunrise to sunset.
tossups.r: That month ends with the new year, Naw-Rúz. For 10 points, name this faith founded by Bahá’u’lláh.

tossups.p: Since Iran’s 1979 revolution, followers of this religion there have been arrested, fired from jobs, and barred from universities, even though Iran is where this religion began more than 150 years ago. They form Iran’s largest non-Muslim religious minority.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion founded by Bahá’u’lláh, whose symbol is a nine-pointed star.

tossups.p: This religion has no clergy, and its members may not take part in partisan politics. Instead, its local communities elect nine-member Spiritual Assemblies to run their affairs, and its worldwide leaders are elected every five years.
tossups.r: Those worldwide leaders form the Universal House of Justice. For 10 points, name this faith founded by Bahá’u’lláh.

tossups.p: Nineteen terraces of gardens climb Mount Carmel around a golden-domed shrine that holds the remains of this religion’s forerunner. In 2008, that shrine and other holy places of this religion in Haifa and near Acre became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this religion led by the Universal House of Justice, which was founded by Bahá’u’lláh.

tossups.p: This religion’s book of laws, the _Kitáb-i-Aqdas_ [“kih-TAHB-ee AHK-dahs”], or “Most Holy Book,” was written by its founder in Acre around 1873, and Shoghi Effendi translated parts of it into English. That book sets a nineteen-day period of fasting.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this faith that sees the Buddha, Jesus, and Muhammad as Manifestations of God.

tossups.p: This religion teaches the “three onenesses” of God, religion, and humanity, and it calls for the equality of women and men and for harmony between science and religion.
tossups.r: It counts Krishna, Zoroaster, and the Buddha as Manifestations of God. For 10 points, name this religion founded in Persia by Bahá’u’lláh.

clues.t: Founded by Bahá’u’lláh (“Glory of God”), a Persian nobleman, in the 1800s
Led by the Universal House of Justice, an elected body of nine, on Mount Carmel in Haifa, Israel
Sees Abraham, Moses, Zoroaster, Krishna, the Buddha, Jesus, and Muhammad as Manifestations of God
Teaches the unity of all religions: the “three onenesses” of God, religion, and humanity
Began in Persia (Iran) in the 1800s
Its forerunner, the Báb (“the Gate”), announced his mission in Shiraz in 1844 and was executed in Tabriz in 1850
Shoghi Effendi, ʻAbdu’l-Bahá’s grandson, was its Guardian from 1921 to 1957
ʻAbdu’l-Bahá, the founder’s eldest son, led it from 1892 to 1921; his 1911 speeches became _Paris Talks_
Its calendar has 19 months of 19 days; followers fast from sunrise to sunset during the last month, just before the New Year, Naw-Rúz
The _Kitáb-i-Íqán_, or _Book of Certitude_, says God sends messengers one after another (“progressive revelation”)
Ridván, a 12-day spring festival, marks the founder’s 1863 announcement in a Baghdad garden that he was God’s new messenger
Its symbol is a nine-pointed star, and its Houses of Worship all have nine sides
Its followers are Iran’s largest non-Muslim minority and have been persecuted there, especially since the 1979 revolution
The founder’s _Kitáb-i-Aqdas_ (“Most Holy Book,” about 1873) is its book of laws; Shoghi Effendi translated parts of it
After Shoghi Effendi died in 1957, the Hands of the Cause guided it through the Ten Year Crusade (1953–1963)
The founder’s last major book, _Epistle to the Son of the Wolf_, was addressed to a cleric whose father persecuted his followers
The founder also wrote the mystical _Seven Valleys_ and _The Hidden Words_
The founder spent his last 24 years as a prisoner and exile around Acre; his shrine at Bahjí is the Qiblih that followers face in prayer
In 1852 the founder was chained in Tehran’s Síyáh-Chál (“Black Pit”) dungeon, where his mission began
The golden-domed Shrine of the Báb sits among 19 garden terraces on Mount Carmel, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site (2008)
The Lotus Temple in New Delhi, designed by Fariborz Sahba, has 27 marble-clad “petals”
Its oldest surviving House of Worship is in Wilmette, Illinois; ʻAbdu’l-Bahá laid its cornerstone in 1912
It has no clergy, members avoid partisan politics, and communities elect nine-member Spiritual Assemblies
Ayyám-i-Há: four or five extra calendar days set aside for gifts and charity

trap.title: Religion, not its prophet
trap.body: This religion grew out of an earlier movement led by the Báb, whose followers were called Bábís, so early clues about “the Gate,” Shiraz, or 1844 can lure you into saying “Bábism.” Players also blurt out a person, like Bahá’u’lláh or ʻAbdu’l-Bahá, when the question wants the religion. And because it began in Iran, some players guess Zoroastrianism or Shia Islam.
trap.fix: If the question asks for “this religion” or “this faith” and mentions the Universal House of Justice, Haifa, Shoghi Effendi, or a nine-pointed star, answer “Bahá’í Faith.” Say “the Báb” or “Bahá’u’lláh” only when it asks for “this man” or “this prophet.”

qb.tip: QBReader returned no Middle School/Easy High School or Regular High School tossups for “Santeria” at any difficulty, and a follow-up search on “orisha” also came back empty, so this topic is written from reference sources (Wikipedia, Britannica) instead.

sample.note: no real QBReader tossups were found for this answer line; the clue breakdown comes from reference sources instead

tossups.p: In 1993, the U.S. Supreme Court sided with a Hialeah, Florida, congregation of this religion in a case protecting its animal-sacrifice rituals under the First Amendment. Diviners in this religion called babalawos [“bah-bah-LAH-wohs”] interpret messages from spirits using a system called Ifá [“ee-FAH”].
tossups.r: Those spirits, called orishas, are each linked to a Catholic saint. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that blends Yoruba spirit worship with Catholicism.

tossups.p: This religion blends Yoruba tradition with Spiritism, a nineteenth-century movement built around contacting the dead, and with Catholicism, the only religion legally permitted in Spanish colonial Cuba. Ancestor spirits called egun are honored separately from this religion’s orishas, who are each linked to a Catholic saint.
tossups.r: Priests called santeros and priestesses called santeras lead its ceremonies. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that developed among enslaved Yoruba people.

tossups.p: Full initiation into this religion, called the asiento, is a seven-day ceremony after which the new initiate, called an iyawó [“ee-yah-WOH”], traditionally dresses only in white for a full year. Its diviners read messages from the orishas using cowrie shells or the Ifá system.
tossups.r: Those orishas are each linked to a Catholic saint. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that blends Yoruba spirit worship with Catholicism.

tossups.p: Sacred stones called otanes, believed to hold an orisha’s power, are kept in covered porcelain tureens on this religion’s home altars. Offerings called ebbó [“eh-BOH”], including fruit, rum, and candles, are believed to feed the orishas and keep a spiritual energy called aché flowing.
tossups.r: Priests called santeros and priestesses called santeras tend these altars. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that blends Yoruba tradition with Catholicism.

tossups.p: A spiritual energy called aché [“ah-SHAY”] is said to flow through people, animals, and sacred objects in this religion, strengthened through proper ritual and offerings called ebbó. Diviners called babalawos interpret the will of this religion’s orishas using the Ifá system.
tossups.r: Each orisha is linked to a Catholic saint. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that developed among enslaved Yoruba people in Cuba.

tossups.p: Double-headed drums called batá [“bah-TAH”], played in matching sets of three sizes, call the orishas to ceremonies known as toques de santo [“TOH-kays deh SAHN-toh”] in this religion. Priests called santeros and priestesses called santeras lead these drumming ceremonies.
tossups.r: Its spirits, called orishas, are each linked to a Catholic saint. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that blends Yoruba tradition with Catholicism.

tossups.p: Changó [“chahn-GOH”], this religion’s orisha of lightning and fire, is identified with the Catholic Santa Bárbara. That pairing reflects how enslaved Yoruba people in Cuba hid their orishas behind Catholic saints under Spanish colonial rule.
tossups.r: A madrina or padrino, meaning “godmother” or “godfather,” sponsors each new initiate into this religion. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion.

tossups.p: Yemayá [“yeh-mah-YAH”], this religion’s orisha of the sea and motherhood, is identified with Our Lady of Regla. Her fellow orisha Ochún [“oh-CHOON”], linked to rivers and love, is identified with Cuba’s patron saint, Our Lady of Charity.
tossups.r: Both are honored alongside a distant creator, Olodumare. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that blends Yoruba orisha worship with Catholicism.

tossups.p: Elegguá [“eh-leh-GWAH”], this religion’s guardian of the crossroads, is usually honored first in ceremonies and is linked to the Holy Child of Atocha. Other orishas in this religion include the warrior-smith Ogún and the storm god Changó.
tossups.r: Each is identified with a Catholic saint. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that developed among enslaved Yoruba people in Cuba.

tossups.p: Obatalá, this religion’s orisha of truth, justice, and creation, is often linked to Our Lady of Mercy. Oyá, its orisha of wind, lightning, and cemeteries, is sometimes linked to Our Lady of Candelaria.
tossups.r: Both orishas trace back to Yoruba tradition in West Africa. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that blends that tradition with Catholicism.

tossups.p: This religion is one of several Afro-Cuban “reglas,” or religious orders, that split along different West and Central African lines; the separate, Kongo-rooted Palo is one example. This religion’s own roots trace specifically to the Yoruba people of West Africa.
tossups.r: Priests called santeros and priestesses called santeras lead its ceremonies honoring spirits called orishas. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that blends Yoruba tradition with Catholicism.

tossups.p: A babalawo, a senior diviner in this religion, interprets the will of its spirits using the Ifá system, while other diviners read patterns cast with cowrie shells. These diviners help ordinary believers understand messages from orishas such as Changó and Yemayá.
tossups.r: Each orisha is linked to a Catholic saint in this religion. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban faith that developed among enslaved Yoruba people in Cuba.

tossups.p: Ancestor spirits called egun are honored at their own household altars in this religion, kept separate from altars for the orishas. Sacred stones called otanes, believed to hold an orisha’s power, are kept in covered porcelain tureens.
tossups.r: Priests called santeros and priestesses called santeras maintain these altars. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion.

tossups.p: Ceremonies in this religion called toques de santo feature batá drumming meant to call down one of its orishas, who may possess a dancer. Priests called santeros and priestesses called santeras lead these ceremonies.
tossups.r: Each orisha this religion honors is linked to a Catholic saint. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that developed among enslaved Yoruba people in Cuba.

tossups.p: Believers in this religion honor a distant creator god, Olodumare, and a spiritual energy called aché. Its spirits, called orishas, are each linked to a Catholic saint, and priests called santeros and priestesses called santeras lead its drumming ceremonies.
tossups.r: It developed among enslaved Yoruba people in nineteenth-century Cuba. For 10 points, name this Afro-Cuban religion that blends Yoruba spirit worship with Roman Catholicism.

clues.t: A religion that developed among enslaved Yoruba people in 19th-century Cuba
Believers honor spirits called orishas, who each have their own powers and personality
Priests called santeros and priestesses called santeras lead ceremonies of drumming and dance
Each orisha is also linked to a Catholic saint, a legacy of worshipping in secret under Spanish rule
A distant supreme creator, Olodumare (or Olorun), rarely receives offerings directly
Changó, orisha of lightning and fire, is identified with the Catholic Santa Bárbara
Yemayá, orisha of the sea and motherhood, is identified with Our Lady of Regla
Ochún, orisha of rivers and love, is linked to Cuba’s patron saint, Our Lady of Charity
Elegguá, guardian of the crossroads, is often honored first and is linked to the Holy Child of Atocha
A madrina or padrino, meaning “godmother” or “godfather,” sponsors and guides each new initiate
Double-headed batá drums, played in sets of three sizes, call the orishas to ceremonies called toques
Obatalá, orisha of truth, justice, and creation, is often linked to Our Lady of Mercy
Oyá, orisha of wind, lightning, and cemeteries, is sometimes linked to Our Lady of Candelaria
Ogún, orisha of iron and war, watches over blacksmiths and other metalworkers
A babalawo is a senior diviner who interprets messages from the orishas using the Ifá system
Diviners also read patterns cast with cowrie shells to answer questions on an orisha’s behalf
Full initiation, the asiento, is a seven-day ceremony after which a new initiate is called an iyawó
A newly initiated iyawó traditionally dresses only in white for a full year afterward
Sacred stones called otanes, believed to hold an orisha’s power, are kept in covered porcelain tureens
Offerings called ebbó — fruit, rum, candles, and sometimes animals — are believed to feed the orishas
A spiritual energy called aché is said to flow through people, animals, plants, and sacred objects alike
This religion blends Yoruba tradition not just with Catholicism but also with Spiritism, a 19th-century movement focused on contacting the dead
A 1993 Supreme Court case over animal sacrifice, brought by a Hialeah, Florida congregation of this faith, affirmed its followers’ religious-freedom rights
Ancestor spirits, called egun, are honored at their own household altars, separate from the orishas

trap.title: Orishas aren’t the religion
trap.body: Nearly every clue names a specific orisha (Changó, Yemayá, Elegguá) or a Catholic saint standing in for one, which tempts players to blurt that name instead of the religion. This faith is also easy to confuse with Haitian Voodoo/Vodou (whose spirits are lwa, not orishas) or with Cuba’s other “reglas,” like the separate Kongo-rooted Palo.
trap.fix: If the question asks “name this religion” and mentions orishas, santeros, or babalawos, answer “Santería.” Say the orisha’s own name only when the question asks for “this spirit” or “this god.” Voodoo’s spirits are lwa; this religion’s are orishas.

sample.note: the 10 real QBReader tossups for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: This man was born in the “Year of the Elephant,” when an army that included an elephant marched on his hometown. Orphaned by the age of six, he was raised by his grandfather and then by his uncle Abu Talib.
tossups.r: Muslims believe the angel Gabriel later revealed the Quran to him. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam, born in Mecca around 570.

tossups.p: As a young man, this trader was known as al-Amin [“al-ah-MEEN”], or “the trustworthy.” A wealthy widow named Khadija [“kah-DEE-jah”] hired him to lead her trading caravan to Syria and later married him, and she became the first person to accept his religious message.
tossups.r: His sayings are collected in the hadith. For 10 points, name this man, whom Muslims regard as the final prophet.

tossups.p: While this man was meditating in a cave on Mount Hira [“hih-RAH”] around the year 610, Muslims believe an angel commanded him to “Read!” He answered that he could not read, but the angel repeated the command and taught him the first verses of a holy book.
tossups.r: That angel was Gabriel, or Jibril, and that book is the Quran. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam.

tossups.p: To escape persecution by the Quraysh [“koo-RAYSH”] tribe, some early followers of this man fled across the Red Sea to the Christian kingdom of Aksum, whose king protected them. Those followers had accepted this man’s teaching that there is only one God, which angered the leaders of Mecca.
tossups.r: In 622, he and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina in the Hijra. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam.

tossups.p: Muslims believe that on a heavenly steed named Buraq [“boo-RAHK”], this man traveled in one night to “the farthest mosque” in Jerusalem and then rose through the heavens in the Mi’raj [“mih-RAHJ”]. According to tradition, Moses urged him on that journey to ask God to reduce the number of daily prayers, which became five.
tossups.r: This man later led his followers from Mecca to Medina. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam.

tossups.p: During one journey, this man and his friend Abu Bakr hid for three days in the cave of Thawr [“THOWR”] while enemies searched for them. That 622 journey, called the Hijra [“HIJ-rah”], marks the first year of the Islamic calendar.
tossups.r: His destination, once called Yathrib [“YATH-rib”], became known as Medina. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam.

tossups.p: This man drafted a charter, often called the Constitution of Medina, that united that city’s Muslims, Jews, and other groups as one community. The people of Medina who welcomed him were called the Ansar [“ahn-SAR”], or “helpers,” while those who moved there with him were the Muhajirun [“moo-HAH-jih-roon”].
tossups.r: This man had left Mecca for Medina in the Hijra. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam, the “Seal of the Prophets.”

tossups.p: In 624, this man led about 300 followers to victory over a larger army from Mecca at the Battle of Badr [“BAH-der”]. That same year, the direction Muslims face in prayer changed from Jerusalem to the Kaaba in Mecca.
tossups.r: This man’s sayings and actions are recorded in the hadith. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam, who moved from Mecca to Medina.

tossups.p: When an army of about 10,000 besieged Medina in 627, this man’s followers dug a long trench on the advice of Salman the Persian, and the attackers eventually gave up. That clash is called the Battle of the Trench, or the Battle of the Ditch.
tossups.r: Muslims call him the “Seal of the Prophets.” For 10 points, name this man, who Muslims believe received the Quran from Gabriel.

tossups.p: When a rumor spread that this man’s son-in-law Uthman had been killed, his followers swore the Pledge of the Tree. This man then signed the Treaty of Hudaybiyyah [“hoo-day-BEE-yah”] in 628, a truce with the Quraysh that let Muslims make a pilgrimage to Mecca the next year.
tossups.r: Two years later, he returned to his birthplace, Mecca, with little fighting. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam.

tossups.p: After the Quraysh broke a truce, this man led about 10,000 followers into Mecca in 630 with little fighting, pardoned most of his old enemies, and removed the idols from the Kaaba. Years earlier, he had defeated the Quraysh at the Battle of Badr.
tossups.r: Muslims say “peace be upon him” after this man’s name. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam.

tossups.p: This man gave his Farewell Sermon near Mount Arafat during his only Hajj in 632. He died a few months later in Medina and was buried there, at a spot now inside a great mosque named for him, beneath a famous green dome.
tossups.r: His father-in-law Abu Bakr then became the first caliph. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam.

tossups.p: A North African dynasty that ruled Egypt until Saladin [“SAL-uh-din”] ended it was named for this man’s daughter Fatima. Fatima’s husband, Ali, was this man’s cousin, and Shia Muslims believe Ali should have been this man’s first successor.
tossups.r: Sunni Muslims take their name from his example, or Sunnah. For 10 points, name this prophet of Islam, who moved from Mecca to Medina in 622.

tossups.p: Out of respect, most Muslims, especially Sunnis, avoid making any pictures of this man, and many say “peace be upon him” after his name. His sayings and actions are recorded in collections called hadith.
tossups.r: The Shahada declares that there is no god but God and that this man is God’s messenger. For 10 points, name this final prophet of Islam.

tossups.p: Muslims call 619 the “Year of Sorrow” in this man’s life, because both his first wife, Khadija, and his uncle and protector, Abu Talib, died that year. Without his uncle’s protection, this man faced growing danger from the Quraysh [“koo-RAYSH”] leaders of his hometown.
tossups.r: Three years later, he left Mecca for Medina. For 10 points, name this prophet, whom Muslims call the “Seal of the Prophets.”

clues.t: Prophet of Islam; real giveaways often call him the “founder of Islam”
Muslims believe the angel Gabriel (Jibril) revealed the Quran to him over about 23 years
Born in Mecca around 570; its leaders opposed his preaching
Muslims call him the “Seal of the Prophets,” the last prophet God sent
Muslims believe Gabriel came to him in a cave on Mount Hira around 610 and said “Read!”; he replied that he could not read
The Hijra (622): he and his followers moved from Mecca to Medina, year 1 of the Islamic calendar
His sayings and actions are recorded in the hadith; his example is called the Sunnah
Member of the Quraysh tribe, whose leaders in Mecca persecuted him and his followers
His first wife, Khadija, a wealthy merchant, hired him to lead her caravan and was the first to accept his message
Out of respect, most Muslims, especially Sunnis, avoid making any pictures of him
The Shahada, first of the Five Pillars, says there is no god but God and that he is God’s messenger
Muslims say or write “peace be upon him” (PBUH) after his name
Died in Medina in 632 and was buried in the Prophet’s Mosque, under its Green Dome
Isra and Mi’raj: Muslims believe he rode Buraq to Jerusalem by night and rose to heaven, where the five daily prayers were set
Treaty of Hudaybiyyah (628): a truce with the Quraysh, after his followers swore the Pledge of the Tree
Wrote the Constitution of Medina, uniting the city’s Muslims, Jews, and other groups as one community
Born in the “Year of the Elephant,” when an army with an elephant attacked Mecca
Orphaned young, he was raised by his grandfather and then his uncle Abu Talib; as a trader he was called al-Amin, “the trustworthy”
Some early followers fled persecution to the Christian kingdom of Aksum (Abyssinia), whose king protected them
Year of Sorrow (619): his wife Khadija and his uncle Abu Talib both died
Ansar (“helpers”) were the Medina locals who welcomed him; the Muhajirun were the Meccans who moved with him
Battle of the Trench (627): on Salman the Persian’s advice, his followers dug a trench to defend Medina
Took Mecca in 630 with little fighting, pardoned most enemies, and cleared the idols from the Kaaba
His daughter Fatima married his cousin Ali; the Fatimid dynasty was named for her
Defeated a larger Meccan army at the Battle of Badr (624); that year the direction of prayer changed from Jerusalem to Mecca
Gave his Farewell Sermon at Mount Arafat during his only Hajj, in 632
After his death, his father-in-law Abu Bakr became the first caliph; Shia Muslims believe his cousin Ali should have led

trap.title: Which Muhammad? Which prophet?
trap.body: Many famous people share his name: one real answer line says do not accept “Muhammad Ali,” the boxer, who also showed up in this search, and Elijah Muhammad led the Nation of Islam in the 1900s. Saying just “the Prophet” earns only a prompt, because Islam honors many prophets, including Abraham, Moses, and Jesus. Clues about his family can also tempt an early buzz of Ali, his cousin and son-in-law, or Abu Bakr, his father-in-law and the first caliph.
trap.fix: Wait for a clue that points to him alone: the cave of Hira, Gabriel revealing the Quran, the Hijra to Medina, or the “Seal of the Prophets.” Then give his name, not a title or a relative.
trap.line: Real answer line: (Abu al-Qasim) Muhammad (ibn ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim) (do not accept “Muhammad Ali”)

topics.name: Book of Revelation
topics.kicker: Last book of the New Testament · Visions of the end of the world
topics.briefing: The Book of Revelation is one of the most vivid books in the Bible. A man named John, on the Greek island of Patmos, describes visions of a scroll with seven seals, the Four Horsemen, a seven-headed red dragon, and the mysterious number 666, and the book ends with a shining New Jerusalem coming down from heaven. Its other name, the Apocalypse, comes from a Greek word meaning “unveiling.”

qb.tip: All 3 results are this book, so the sample adds 9 Regular High School tossups, and 11 of the 12 answer lines say “do not accept or prompt on Revelations.”

sample.note: 12 real QBReader tossups (3 Middle School/Easy High School + 9 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: The narrator of this book is told by an angel to eat a little scroll, which tastes as sweet as honey in his mouth but turns bitter in his stomach. Earlier in this book, 144,000 people from the twelve tribes of Israel are sealed as servants of God.
tossups.r: Seven angels blow seven trumpets after the seventh seal is opened in this book. For 10 points, name this last book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: When the third angel in this book blows his trumpet, a blazing star named Wormwood falls from heaven and turns a third of the rivers and springs bitter. At the second trumpet, something like a great burning mountain is thrown into the sea.
tossups.r: Its author, John, says he saw its visions on the Greek island of Patmos. For 10 points, name this final book of the Bible.

tossups.p: In this book, the church in Laodicea [“lay-oh-dih-SEE-uh”] is scolded for being “lukewarm,” neither hot nor cold, while the church in Ephesus is told it has abandoned the love it had at first. The message to Laodicea also says, “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock.”
tossups.r: Those are two of the seven churches of Asia that receive messages near the start of this book. For 10 points, name this book written by John of Patmos.

tossups.p: In this book, locusts with human faces, lions’ teeth, and tails like scorpions rise from a bottomless pit when the fifth trumpet sounds, and they torment people for five months. Their king is an angel called Abaddon [“uh-BAD-un”] in Hebrew and Apollyon [“uh-POL-yun”] in Greek.
tossups.r: Earlier, the Four Horsemen ride out as the first four seals are opened. For 10 points, name this final book of the New Testament, which describes the end of the world.

tossups.p: In this book, no one in heaven or on earth is worthy to open a scroll sealed with seven seals until the “Lion of the tribe of Judah” appears as a Lamb with seven horns and seven eyes.
tossups.r: As the Lamb opens the first four seals, the Four Horsemen ride out. For 10 points, name this book of the Bible attributed to John of Patmos.

tossups.p: In this book, the one seated on the heavenly throne looks like jasper and carnelian [“kar-NEEL-yun”], with a rainbow like an emerald around the throne. Four winged living creatures stand around that throne, before which lies a sea of glass like crystal.
tossups.r: Later, the narrator sees a new heaven, a new earth, and a holy city called New Jerusalem. For 10 points, name this final book of the Bible.

tossups.p: In this book, a great red dragon with seven heads and ten horns threatens a woman and her newborn child, who is carried up to God. The archangel Michael and his angels then defeat the dragon in a war in heaven.
tossups.r: That dragon is identified as Satan. For 10 points, name this last book of the New Testament, whose Four Horsemen are often called Conquest, War, Famine, and Death.

tossups.p: In this book, a woman dressed in purple and scarlet rides a scarlet beast and holds a golden cup, and her forehead bears the name “Babylon the Great.” An angel later announces that “Babylon the great is fallen,” and merchants weep over the city’s ruin.
tossups.r: Many scholars think “Babylon” was a code name for Rome. For 10 points, name this final book of the New Testament, written by John of Patmos.

tossups.p: When the sixth seal is opened in this book, a great earthquake strikes, the sun turns black, the moon turns red, and the stars fall to earth like figs from a tree. Afterward, four angels hold back the four winds while servants of God are sealed on their foreheads.
tossups.r: Those servants number 144,000. For 10 points, name this last book of the Bible, which also features the Four Horsemen.

tossups.p: At the end of this book, a river of the water of life flows from God’s throne, and beside it grows a tree of life that bears twelve kinds of fruit, with leaves for the healing of the nations. Each of the twelve gates of the holy city in that vision is made from a single pearl.
tossups.r: That city, the New Jerusalem, has a street of pure gold. For 10 points, name this final book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: When the sixth angel pours out his bowl in this book, the Euphrates [“yoo-FRAY-teez”] River dries up to prepare the way for “the kings of the east.” Those kings are then gathered for a final battle at a place called, in Hebrew, Armageddon [“ar-muh-GED-un”].
tossups.r: This book also introduces the number of the beast, 666. For 10 points, name this last book of the Bible.

tossups.p: Ingmar Bergman’s film _The Seventh Seal_ takes its title from this book, and Albrecht Dürer [“DYUR-er”] made a famous woodcut of four riders from it. The words “King of Kings, and Lord of Lords” in Handel’s “Hallelujah” chorus also come from this book.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this final book of the New Testament, in which the Four Horsemen ride out as seals are opened.

tossups.p: Many scholars think a number in this book is a code for the emperor Nero, since the Hebrew letters of “Nero Caesar” add up to it. In this book, no one can buy or sell without a mark on the right hand or forehead.
tossups.r: That number, 666, is the number of the beast. For 10 points, name this last book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: Near the end of this book, an angel binds Satan with a great chain and locks him in a bottomless pit for a thousand years, a period that gives its name to beliefs called millennialism. Satan is finally thrown into a lake of fire.
tossups.r: This book ends with a vision of a new heaven and a new earth. For 10 points, name this final book of the New Testament.

tossups.p: This book’s narrator says he was “in the Spirit on the Lord’s day” when a loud voice behind him, like a trumpet, told him to write down what he saw and send it to seven churches in Asia. He then saw seven golden lampstands.
tossups.r: A voice in this book declares, “I am the Alpha and the Omega.” For 10 points, name this book by John of Patmos, the last book of the Bible.

clues.t: The last book of the New Testament, and so the final book of the Christian Bible
Its author, a man named John, says he saw its visions on the Greek island of Patmos
Its visions describe the end of the world and God’s final victory over evil
Opening the first four seals releases the Four Horsemen, often called Conquest, War, Famine, and Death
A scroll sealed with seven seals is opened one seal at a time by the Lamb
Opens with messages to seven churches in Asia Minor, including Ephesus, Sardis, and Philadelphia
After the seventh seal is opened, seven angels blow seven trumpets
666 is the “number of the beast”; many scholars think it was a code for the emperor Nero
It ends with a new heaven, a new earth, and the New Jerusalem, a holy city with gates of pearl and a street of gold
144,000 servants of God, 12,000 from each tribe of Israel, are sealed on their foreheads
A voice declares, “I am the Alpha and the Omega,” the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet
The Euphrates River dries up for “the kings of the east,” who gather for battle at Armageddon
The narrator eats a little scroll that is sweet as honey in his mouth but bitter in his stomach
At the third trumpet, a blazing star named Wormwood makes a third of the rivers and springs bitter
At the fifth trumpet, locusts with human faces and scorpion tails, led by the angel Abaddon, torment people for five months
Only the Lamb, called the “Lion of the tribe of Judah,” is worthy to open the sealed scroll
God on the throne looks like jasper and carnelian, with an emerald rainbow and a sea of glass before the throne
At the sixth seal, the sun turns black, the moon turns red, and stars fall to earth like figs
A woman named “Babylon the Great” rides a scarlet beast and holds a golden cup; many think “Babylon” stood for Rome
A river of the water of life flows from God’s throne past a tree of life with twelve kinds of fruit and healing leaves
An angel chains Satan in a bottomless pit for a thousand years (the millennium); later Satan is thrown into a lake of fire
A great red dragon with seven heads loses a war in heaven to the archangel Michael and his angels
The church in Laodicea is scolded for being “lukewarm,” neither hot nor cold
Inspired Bergman’s film _The Seventh Seal_, Dürer’s woodcut of four riders, and words in Handel’s “Hallelujah” chorus
The narrator was “in the Spirit on the Lord’s day” when a trumpet-like voice spoke, and he saw seven golden lampstands

trap.title: Revelation, not Revelations!
trap.body: The book’s title is singular. In 11 of the 12 real answer lines in our sample, “Revelations” or “Book of Revelations” is marked “do not accept or prompt,” so one extra letter loses the tossup. Players also confuse it with the Gospel of John (one real line refuses “Apocalypse of John” for the Gospel) and the Book of Daniel, the Hebrew Bible’s book of beast visions.
trap.fix: Say “Book of Revelation” or just “Revelation.” “Apocalypse of John” is accepted too, but plain “Apocalypse” is accepted by some answer lines and only prompted by others. Seals, trumpets, horsemen, Patmos, and 666 mean Revelation; the lions’ den and the writing on the wall mean Daniel.
trap.line: Real answer line: Book of Revelation [prompt on the Bible or the New Testament before mentioned; do not accept or prompt on “Book of Revelations”]

topics.name: Jerusalem
topics.kicker: Holy city of three faiths · Western Wall and Dome of the Rock
topics.briefing: Inside one small walled Old City you can find the Western Wall, where Jews pray beside the remains of their ancient Temple’s platform; the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, where Christians believe Jesus was buried; and the golden Dome of the Rock and al-Aqsa Mosque, sacred to Muslims. King David made Jerusalem his capital around 1000 BCE, and since then Babylonians, Romans, Crusaders, and Saladin have all conquered it.

qb.tip: Only 3 results at this level and one is really about Solomon’s Temple, so the sample adds 7 Regular High School tossups; read every answer line, because Temple questions only prompt on “Jerusalem.”

sample.note: 9 real QBReader tossups (2 Middle School/Easy High School + 7 Regular High School, power-marked)

tossups.p: A cave called the Well of Souls lies beneath this city’s Foundation Stone, a rock that Jewish tradition identifies as the site of the Temple’s Holy of Holies. The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik [“AHB-dul MAH-lik”] built a domed shrine over that rock, completed around 691 CE.
tossups.r: That shrine, the golden Dome of the Rock, stands on the Temple Mount. For 10 points, name this city holy to Jews, Christians, and Muslims.

tossups.p: In Islam’s early years, Muslims faced this city when they prayed, making it the first qibla [“KIB-luh”], before the direction of prayer was changed to the Kaaba in Mecca. Muslims believe Muhammad rode the heavenly steed Buraq [“boo-RAHK”] to this city during his Night Journey.
tossups.r: Its al-Aqsa Mosque makes it the third-holiest city in Islam. For 10 points, name this city, also home to the Western Wall.

tossups.p: Twice a year, the paper prayers that visitors tuck into the cracks of a wall in this city are cleared out and buried on the nearby Mount of Olives. That wall survives from the huge platform that Herod the Great built when he enlarged the Second Temple.
tossups.r: That Western Wall is the holiest site where Jews may pray. For 10 points, name this city, which Israel calls its capital.

tossups.p: A carving on Rome’s Arch of Titus shows soldiers carrying a giant menorah taken from this city in 70 CE. Jews fast on Tisha B’Av [“TISH-uh BAHV”] to mourn the destruction of the two Temples that once stood in this city.
tossups.r: Its Temple Mount is now home to the Dome of the Rock and the al-Aqsa Mosque. For 10 points, name this city holy to Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.

tossups.p: After King Nebuchadnezzar II [“neb-uh-kud-NEZ-er”] of Babylon destroyed this city’s First Temple, many of its people were carried off into exile, an event mourned in Psalm 137. About fifty years later, Cyrus the Great allowed the exiles to return and rebuild.
tossups.r: The Second Temple was then built on the same hill. For 10 points, name this city where King Solomon built the First Temple.

tossups.p: Godfrey of Bouillon [“boo-YOHN”] became the first ruler of a Crusader state named for this city after knights of the First Crusade captured it in July 1099. His brother Baldwin then became that state’s first crowned king.
tossups.r: Saladin retook this city in 1187, setting off the Third Crusade. For 10 points, name this city that the Crusades fought to control.

tossups.p: After defeating Guy of Lusignan [“LOO-zeen-yahn”] at the Horns of Hattin [“hah-TEEN”] in 1187, Saladin captured this city. During the Third Crusade, Richard the Lionheart twice came within a short march of this city but turned back.
tossups.r: A truce later let Christian pilgrims visit this city. For 10 points, name this holy city, the main target of the Crusades.

tossups.p: The Knights Templar took their name from their headquarters on this city’s Temple Mount, in a mosque that Crusaders believed was the Temple of Solomon. The Knights Hospitaller began as a group caring for sick pilgrims at a hospital in this city.
tossups.r: Both orders later guarded Christians traveling to this city. For 10 points, name this holy city, home to the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

tossups.p: Jews end the Passover Seder [“SAY-der”] and the closing service of Yom Kippur with the words “Next year in” this city. Many Jewish weddings end with breaking a glass, often explained as a way to remember the destroyed Temple in this city.
tossups.r: Most synagogues are built so that worshippers face this city. For 10 points, name this city, home to the Western Wall.

tossups.p: This city’s walled Old City is traditionally divided into Jewish, Christian, Muslim, and Armenian Quarters. The Ottoman sultan Suleiman [“SOO-lay-mahn”] the Magnificent built most of the walls around that Old City in the 1500s, including the Damascus Gate.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this city whose Old City holds the Western Wall, the Dome of the Rock, and the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.

tossups.p: The Roman emperor Hadrian rebuilt this city as a colony named Aelia Capitolina [“EE-lee-uh kap-ih-toh-LEE-nuh”], and after the Bar Kokhba [“bar KOKH-buh”] revolt, Jews were banned from entering it. Decades earlier, the Roman general Titus had besieged this city in 70 CE.
tossups.r: That siege ended with the destruction of the Second Temple. For 10 points, name this city, home to the Western Wall.

tossups.p: Muslims call a walled hilltop compound in this city the Haram al-Sharif [“hah-RAHM al-shah-REEF”], or “Noble Sanctuary.” The al-Aqsa Mosque in that compound is named for the “Farthest Mosque” that the Quran mentions in its account of Muhammad’s Night Journey.
tossups.r: Jews call the same hilltop the Temple Mount. For 10 points, name this city, the third-holiest in Islam.

tossups.p: This city was held by the Jebusites [“JEB-yoo-sites”] until King David captured its fortress of Zion, which became known as the City of David, and made the city his capital. David then brought the Ark of the Covenant into this city.
tossups.r: His son Solomon built the First Temple there to house the Ark. For 10 points, name this city, the capital of ancient Israel.

tossups.p: Pilgrims in this city visit the Cenacle [“SEN-uh-kul”], an upper room on Mount Zion traditionally said to be where Jesus ate the Last Supper, and walk the Via Dolorosa [“VEE-uh doh-luh-ROH-suh”], the route Christians believe he took while carrying his cross.
tossups.r: Christians believe Jesus was crucified and buried at the site of its Church of the Holy Sepulchre. For 10 points, name this city that Jesus entered on Palm Sunday.

tossups.p: In 1229, Emperor Frederick II regained this city for the Crusaders through a treaty, without fighting a battle. Nine centuries earlier, the emperor Constantine had ordered a great church built in this city at the place where Christians believe Jesus was buried.
tossups.r: Tradition places Abraham’s near-sacrifice of his son Isaac on its Mount Moriah [“muh-RYE-uh”]. For 10 points, name this city holy to Jews, Christians, and Muslims.

clues.t: A holy city for all three Abrahamic religions: Judaism, Christianity, and Islam
Home of the Western Wall (the Wailing Wall), the holiest site where Jews may pray
Site of the two ancient Jewish Temples, the First Temple and the Second Temple
Islam’s third-holiest city, after Mecca and Medina, because of its al-Aqsa Mosque
The main target of the medieval Crusades
Israel calls it its capital, but that status is disputed; Palestinians also claim its eastern part

King Solomon built the First Temple there to hold the Ark of the Covenant in its Holy of Holies
Under the Dome of the Rock is the Foundation Stone, with a small cave called the Well of Souls beneath it
Islam’s first qibla: early Muslims faced it in prayer before switching to the Kaaba in Mecca
Prayer notes tucked into the Western Wall’s cracks are cleared out twice a year and buried on the Mount of Olives
Herod the Great enlarged the Second Temple’s platform; the Western Wall survives from it
Rome’s Arch of Titus shows the Temple’s menorah being carried off; Jews mourn both Temples on Tisha B’Av
Babylon’s King Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed the First Temple (about 586 BCE); Cyrus the Great later let the exiles return
The First Crusade captured it in 1099; Godfrey of Bouillon became the first ruler of the Crusader kingdom named for it
Saladin won the Battle of Hattin and retook it in 1187, setting off the Third Crusade with Richard the Lionheart
The Knights Templar were named for their headquarters on its Temple Mount; the Knights Hospitaller began at a hospital there
Jews end the Passover Seder and Yom Kippur with the words “Next year in” this city
Its walled Old City has Jewish, Christian, Muslim, and Armenian Quarters; Suleiman the Magnificent built most of the walls

In 1229, Emperor Frederick II regained it for the Crusaders by treaty, without a battle

trap.title: The city or the Temple?
trap.body: Some real tossups about holy sites in this city want the site, not the city. One answer line for the Temple says only “prompt on Jerusalem,” and a middle-school tossup on Solomon’s First Temple says “do not accept or prompt on Second Temple.” Islam clues trip players too: the Kaaba and the Hajj mean Mecca, and the Prophet’s Mosque means Medina.
trap.fix: Listen to the last noun: “this city” means Jerusalem, while “this building,” “this structure,” or “this place” with the Holy of Holies, the Ark, or Hanukkah’s oil means the Temple. The first qibla, al-Aqsa, and the Night Journey point to Jerusalem.
trap.line: Real answer lines: Jerusalem [or Yerushalayim or al-Quds; anti-prompt on Temple Mount] and the Temple [accept First Temple or Second Temple; prompt on Jerusalem]
